svg.text: A day in the life of a packet: receive (RX) and send (TX) on a ConnectX NIC with the mlx5 driver
RX (blue) climbs from the cable to the app. TX (orange) goes down from the app to the cable. Interrupts are red and dashed. Step numbers match the text.
copied from the socket into the app's memory
checks IP + TCP, finds the socket,
queues the data, wakes the app
reads each CQE, wraps the buffer as an skb
(no copy), runs XDP if loaded, then GRO
then re-arm the CQ so the
free the skb, wake the queue
polls the TX and RX CQs (budget 64)
IRQ, one NAPI, one RQ + its SQs
builds the skb and headers, the qdisc
and XPS pick a send queue (SQ)
DMA-maps the data, writes a WQE
takes the next RQ WQE, writes the packet into
that buffer, then writes a CQE
if the CQ is armed: write an EQE,
reads the WQE, then the packet data,
parse headers, steering (flow tables + RSS hash)
picks the RQ, checks checksums, strips VLAN
calculates checksums, TSO cuts big sends
holds packets until the pipeline takes them;
if full: pause / PFC, or drop
RX: find the frame, check the FCS (CRC),
TX: add the preamble and the
RX: recover the clock, turn the signal into bits,
TX: encode, add FEC, turn bits
into an electrical or optical signal
Port: RJ45 (copper BASE-T) or QSFP / OSFP cage (DAC / optical)
read (dashed) = DMA read or CPU read

WQE = work queue entry (a descriptor: “here is a buffer”). CQE = completion queue entry (“done: this many bytes, checksum OK, RSS hash ...”). EQE = event queue entry. skb = the kernel's packet object.
